items.title: Brent back at $106 and the 6-month contract just printed a record: the curve says nobody believes this ends soon
items.idea: Houthi strikes on Saudi airports pushed Brent front-month to $106, while the contract six months out hit a record high. That is the market pricing duration of conflict, not a spike. It happened despite last week's Trump-Putin diesel sanctions relief, which was supposed to cap prices.
items.angle: Back-end strength is the tell: spike risk is fading, structural risk premium is repricing. Supports long-dated energy equities over front-month trades.
items.tweetA: Front-month Brent at $106 is the headline. The 6-month contract at a record is the story. Spikes mean-revert; a curve that reprices the back end is a market saying 'this is the new regime'. $XLE $XOM
items.tweetB: Washington cut a diesel deal with Moscow to lower pump prices and oil went UP. When a policy designed to cap price makes the 6-month contract print a record, the market is reading it as a distress signal, not a solution.

charts.desc: Brent front vs 6-month-out curve at record; diesel near ATH barely moved after the Russia deal

items.title: Russia conceded nothing, got diesel sanctions reversed in hours, without Congress
items.idea: Tina Fordham (Fordham Global Foresight): the Treasury issued a temporary licence within hours, barely a month after Trump signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law backed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. White House also asked the EU to stop delivering weapons to Ukraine via PURL. Markets read it as US desperation: diesel is near its all-time high and barely moved.
items.angle: Sanctions credibility is now a priced variable. If executive licences can undo statute in hours, every sanctions-dependent trade (Urals discounts, shadow fleet, EU gas) carries policy-reversal risk.
items.tweetA: A sanctions law signed a month ago, undone by a Treasury licence in hours, for a concession Russia never made. Diesel didn't blink. The market isn't pricing the deal, it's pricing who needs it more. $MPC $VLO
items.tweetB: Ask the question nobody is asking: if sanctions on Russia can be switched off by licence, what is the discount on Russian barrels actually worth next time? The whole shadow-fleet arbitrage just got a political option attached.

charts.desc: Diesel futures near ATH after Russia deal

items.title: Yanbu bypass: a 7mbpd pipeline that only shipped 3.5-4mbpd from April to July
items.idea: Capital Economics' Jason Tuvey: Saudi East-West pipeline can move 7M b/d but limited export capacity at Yanbu capped crude and product shipments at 3.5-4M b/d from April to July. An Iraqi militia attack there was contained weeks ago; a Houthi attack might not be. Authers: shutting routes that bypass Hormuz could easily take oil past $120.
items.angle: The Hormuz bypass is a bottleneck story, not a capacity story. Half the nameplate is the real number, and it sits next to Houthi range.
items.tweetA: Everyone's 'Hormuz bypass' comfort blanket is a 7M b/d pipeline. Actual exports from Yanbu ran at half that for four months. The insurance policy has a 50% deductible and sits in Houthi range.
items.tweetB: Do the math: if Yanbu is ~3.75M b/d of effective bypass and it goes down while Hormuz stays impaired, $120 isn't a tail, it's arithmetic. Who is long that optionality? $OXY $COP

charts.desc: Capital Economics chart: Yanbu shipments 3.5-4M b/d vs 7M b/d pipeline

items.title: BCA's Papic: the Houthis are rational, Yemen-focused, and have been deliberately gentle on oil
items.idea: Marko Papic: Houthi aim is dominating Yemen, not the region, so they cut deals with external enemies and so far kept energy attacks contained to avoid Washington's crosshairs. BI's Dina Esfandiary: the Saudis have pushed for a US-Iran deal but may feel cornered into urging US escalation vs Iran. Authers: US difficulty with Iran in Hormuz shows military superiority isn't the point.
items.angle: The restraint is a choice, so it is reversible. The key swing variable may be Riyadh's response, not Sanaa's.
items.tweetA: The Houthis keeping oil prices contained is a policy choice, not a capability limit. Choices get revisited when someone pushes them into a corner. Right now the party being cornered is Riyadh.
items.tweetB: Saudi Arabia was the dove. Airports get hit and the dove starts lobbying for escalation on Iran. Second-order effect nobody has in the oil curve: the most pro-deal voice in the region flips.

items.title: Real 10y yields +100bp to 2.88% this year and gold is down only ~3%
items.idea: The Fed under Kevin Warsh is back to hiking, dollar at multi-month highs, real 10y yield up a full point to 2.88%, yet gold is down only about 3% YTD. Its return as of Friday is among the weakest in a decade, behind only 2022. Gavekal's Gave: gold still beats all major bond markets since 2019. TD's McKay sees decoupling from real rates into a new bull in 2027.
items.angle: A 100bp real-yield move should cost gold far more than 3%. The residual is the debasement/central-bank bid, which is the real thesis.
items.tweetA: Real yields up 100bp. Gold down 3%. By the 2022 playbook it should be down 15-20%. Something else is bidding, and it doesn't care about the discount rate. $GLD $GDX
items.tweetB: Gold's worst run in five years is a 3% drawdown. If that's the stress test with hiking Fed, strong dollar and war inflation all against it, what happens the day one of those legs flips?

charts.desc: Gold vs real 10y yield divergence; gold YTD return vs history (weakest since 2022)

items.title: 45% of central banks plan to add gold; mine supply grew only 2%; Sept ETF inflows best since Q1 2022
items.idea: World Gold Council: 45% of policymakers plan to raise gold holdings over the next year, led by China, for geopolitical hedging. Q2 mine output rose just 2% y/y. September gold ETF net inflows were the largest in any month since Q1 2022. UBS's Daniel Major: gold above $4,000 makes miners' FCF attractive but he avoids M&A-prone large caps.
items.angle: Price-insensitive official buyers plus inelastic supply is the floor; ETF inflows say Western money is returning while real yields are still rising.
items.tweetA: Central banks buy gold for reasons that have nothing to do with real yields, and mines can't add supply for years. That's a floor with a ceiling-less supply curve. Western ETFs just started buying too.
items.tweetB: The 45% number is the one to watch: not 45% of central banks hold gold, 45% intend to ADD. In a hiking cycle with a strong dollar. That's what de-dollarization looks like in the data, not in the headlines.

items.title: Wednesday CPI: headline 3.4% to 3.6%, core 2.4% to 2.5% expected, with a Fed already hiking
items.idea: September CPI is due Wednesday. Consensus has headline rising from 3.4% to 3.6% and core from 2.4% to 2.5% on record fuel prices. Authers notes that if the diesel deal works, traders may look through the backward-looking print. Louis Gave: still a 'currency debasement, cash is trash' regime.
items.angle: Core only at 2.5% while the Fed hikes is the odd part: the hikes are an oil-shock response, not a core-inflation one. Policy-error risk if energy rolls over.
items.tweetA: Core CPI at 2.5% and the Fed is hiking. That's not a Fed fighting inflation, it's a Fed fighting an oil shock with a blunt instrument. If crude fades, the hikes look like a policy error in real time.
items.tweetB: Headline 3.6%, core 2.5%: the 110bp gap is the whole trade. Energy goes down, headline converges to core and the hiking cycle loses its excuse. Energy stays up and core eventually follows. Pick your side.

items.title: Goldman: a $20 war premium and restocking demand are keeping crude bid even as Gulf supply adapts
items.idea: Per Daan Struyven's Goldman work: Persian Gulf exports have recovered faster than expected, tanker availability improved, shippers are operating through the disruption. Base case is lower crude, but inventories are still low so buyers are rebuilding buffers, and about $20 of war premium stays embedded. Thin market, several dollars can vanish or reappear on headlines.
items.angle: Goldman's base case is down but the path is headline-driven. Good setup for selling rallies via structure rather than outright shorts.
items.tweetA: Goldman has crude lower on the physical balance and still pays up for a $20 war premium. That's a $20 option on a headline. Option sellers love that; option owners should ask what strike they'd get for free.
items.tweetB: Inventories are low because everyone is restocking at the same time. It's a demand source that disappears the day buffers are rebuilt, and nobody times that. Unwinding of that bid is the underappreciated downside catalyst.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman summaries)
items.title: Goldman: hedge funds raise gross, keep net near the floor, with Mag7 on Prime at a record
items.idea: Pierre Saboureault and Robbie Stankard: gross exposure climbed materially while net stays near the bottom of its recent range, i.e. participation without conviction. Funds sold Info Tech aggressively after the OpenAI revenue scare, yet Mag7 exposure on the Prime book is still a record. CTAs have already sold about two-thirds of their global equity length, buybacks in blackout, retail hesitant.
items.angle: Record Mag7 exposure with record-low net means shorts elsewhere pay for the longs. The index is held up by names nobody will sell.
items.tweetA: Gross up, net at the floor, Mag7 at a record. That's not a bull market, it's a pairs book: long the same seven names, short everything else. Fine until the seven stop working.
items.tweetB: Funds sold tech after the OpenAI revenue scare and still hold record Mag7. Selling the periphery and keeping the core is exactly what you do when you're afraid of being wrong, not afraid of being long.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman summaries)
items.title: Goldman: the squeeze setup exists, but oil and rates have to cooperate first
items.idea: Non-economic buyers are temporarily weaker: CTAs have sold ~2/3 of equity length (cleaner positioning), buybacks about to return from blackout, fundamental net is low, upside call demand firm. Goldman's catch: oil and rates must cooperate before dry powder becomes a sustainable chase higher.
items.angle: Clean CTA positioning plus returning buyback bid is the mechanical support; the macro trigger sits in the same oil complex covered above.
items.tweetA: The setup for an equity squeeze is fully loaded: CTAs flat, buybacks restart, calls bid. The trigger is Brent and the 10-year. Yes, the same Brent printing a 6-month record today. Check your correlations.
items.tweetB: Buybacks coming out of blackout into a market where CTAs already sold two-thirds of their length. The marginal seller is gone and the marginal buyer is about to return. That asymmetry is the trade even if the macro is ugly.

items.title: Econ Nobel to Hall and Woodford: New Keynesian macro finally gets its prize
items.idea: Noah Smith: this year's Nobel went to Bob Hall and Michael Woodford. Hall's 1978 result (consumption changes unpredictable from lagged income) underpins forward-looking expectations; Woodford synthesized sticky-price models into the framework central banks use. Smith argues the 2022-23 'immaculate disinflation' (9% to ~3% without a unemployment surge) was the acid test: a credible Fed commitment moved expectations.
items.angle: The prize lands just as a hiking Fed under Warsh tests the same expectations channel in an oil shock. Credibility is the asset the framework prices.
items.tweetA: The Nobel goes to the people who told central banks: expectations are the policy tool. Good timing. We're about to find out if a hiking Fed can anchor expectations when headline CPI is driven by a war.
items.tweetB: Immaculate disinflation 2023: 9% to 3% with no recession because businesses believed the Fed. Now the Fed is hiking with core at 2.5%. What does credibility do when the Fed is hiking against a supply shock rather than demand?

items.title: Hall's fiscal multiplier: 0.7-1.0 normally, ~1.7 at the zero lower bound
items.idea: Smith cites Hall (2009): government purchase multiplier in the 0.7-1.0 range, around 1.7 when the nominal rate is at zero. Woodford (2011) shows multipliers well above one at the ZLB. Both only hold when the central bank doesn't offset stimulus by raising rates.
items.angle: Rates are now going up, so the ZLB multiplier logic is inverted: fiscal impulse with a hiking Fed is closer to a sub-1 multiplier.
items.tweetA: Hall's 1.7 multiplier required a zero-rate Fed that doesn't offset. Flip it: deficits near 6% of GDP with a Fed hiking. By Hall's own model the multiplier is under 1 and the deficit buys less each year.
items.tweetB: Everyone quotes the Keynesian multiplier from 2009. Nobody asks what it is when the central bank is the one leaning against it. That's the number that matters for the next fiscal package.

items.title: Meta's Muse Wonder Full scores 56 on the AI Intelligence Index: tied with Sonnet 5.5, 2 behind Opus 5.5
items.idea: Artificial Analysis: Muse Wonder Full 56, Wonder 52, up from 48 for Muse Spark 1.3 six weeks ago; ahead of GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon and Claude Fable 5.1 (53 each), behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 58. Terminal-Bench 4.0 jumped 33% to 57%. Cost per Index task $4.52 vs $3.26 (GPT-6 Astra) and $1.99 (Gemini 4 Argon). API $4/M input, $20/M output.
items.angle: Meta went from zero to frontier in 14 months, but at 2x the cost per task of Gemini. Frontier on quality, not on price.
items.tweetA: Meta: 14 months from reboot to the frontier, 8 index points in six weeks. Also $4.52 per task vs $1.99 for Gemini. Frontier performance is being commoditised faster than frontier pricing. $META $GOOGL
items.tweetB: Four labs tied at 53-56 on the index. When four models are indistinguishable, the moat isn't the model. It's distribution, and Meta has 3.5B users. That's the real bull case, not the benchmark.

items.source: Michael Parekh / AI: Reset to Zero
items.title: Memory moved into the model: Meta puts context compaction inside the weights, not the harness
items.idea: Wang/Zuckerberg on Cheeky Pint: instead of external harness logic that swaps long/short-term memory as context fills, the model manages its own compaction ('Active Memory'). Parekh calls compaction 'the new 640K' and says what survives varies from run to run. Also 'Active Focus': persistence on goals, trying other approaches rather than stalling.
items.angle: If in-model memory works, long-horizon agents stop being brittle, which expands the addressable work per token (more tokens, more compute demand).
items.tweetA: 'Compaction is the new 640K' is a good line. If the model, not the scaffold, owns its memory, agents run for days. A task that lasts days burns 1000x the tokens of a chat. Memory and context is a demand multiplier. $MU $NVDA
items.tweetB: The agent stack's fragile part was never reasoning, it was forgetting. Whoever solves memory first gets retention, which is where Muse is weakest vs ChatGPT at 14 days.

items.source: Michael Parekh / AI: Reset to Zero
items.title: $15B a year to run 1GW, $50-60B to build it, and Zuckerberg wrote the check before seeing the model
items.idea: Zuckerberg: a 1GW cluster costs ~$15B a year to run, $50-60B upfront capex, for one part of training. Meta planned Prometheus (Ohio, >1GW) and Hyperion (Louisiana, scaling to 5GW) in 2023-24; the $100-200B check was approved at end of 2025 before Wang's team had a model. Zuck: failure requires all of AI to fail. He has ~61% of votes on ~14% of economics.
items.angle: Capex as founder-control artefact. $15B/GW/yr is also a useful unit for modelling any AI buildout.
items.tweetA: $15B a year to operate one gigawatt. Hyperion scales to five. That's $75B of annual run cost before anyone writes a line of revenue. Only a founder with 61% of the votes can underwrite that. $META
items.tweetB: Zuckerberg's hedge is 'if AI fails, everyone fails'. It's a good argument for Meta and a terrible one for the sector: it means the entire capex cycle shares one correlated downside.

items.source: Michael Parekh / AI: Reset to Zero
items.title: Only 14% of OpenRouter usage ran through the top-10 models in Q3, down from 55% in Q1 last year
items.idea: The Information's Martin Peers (via Parekh): everyone claims the frontier now, and users trade down to 'good enough' cheaper models. 14% of OpenRouter usage went through the ten highest-quality models in Q3, vs 55% in Q1 2025. Peers: the main impact of Muse Wonder on Muse might be on Meta's costs.
items.angle: Frontier labs sell the top 14% of the token market. Demand is in the long tail, which favours cheap inference and custom silicon.
items.tweetA: 55% to 14% in six quarters. The market for the best model is shrinking relative to the market for a model that's good enough. The frontier labs are spending $100B for the minority of tokens.
items.tweetB: OpenRouter measures developers shopping per token, which is the most price-elastic buyer there is. If they're trading down, enterprise procurement is about 12 months behind. That's the margin pressure for API pricing.

items.source: Michael Parekh / AI: Reset to Zero
items.title: Alibaba's Qwen3.8 is 2.4T params (95B active); Qwen 4.5/5 projected at 5-10T
items.idea: Alibaba open-sourced Qwen3.8 in August at 2.4T parameters with 95B active. Next-gen models are projected at 5-10T. Parekh's contrast: US labs don't disclose sizes (Meta says each pretrain is roughly 4-5x the last); Chinese labs disclose and open-source.
items.angle: China competes on scale and openness, the US on undisclosed frontier and capex. A size race where one side publishes weights.
items.tweetA: China is publishing parameter counts and weights. The US labs are hiding both. One side is building an ecosystem, the other a product moat. 10T open-weights model is the real stress test for $50 billion of closed-model capex.
items.tweetB: 95B active out of 2.4T. Mixture-of-experts means the inference bill scales with active parameters, not headline size. China's 5-10T models won't cost 5x to run. Check that against the closed labs' pricing.

items.title: Checkonchain: 'bear market PTSD' still visible across onchain, ETF and derivatives metrics
items.idea: Only the preview is public (the full note is paywalled): Checkonchain argues there is still a tonne of fear in Bitcoin and investors can't believe the bottom may be in. Recency and confirmation bias keep people from accepting disconfirming data. Those who survived the bear market make fear-driven mistakes early in the recovery.
items.angle: Contrarian sentiment marker from a data-heavy source. Charts inside the paid piece: worth opening.
items.tweetA: The bottom is the point where the data says 'in' and the crowd still says 'not yet'. Checkonchain says fear is still visible in on-chain, ETF and derivative metrics. Early bull markets are climbed by people who don't believe in them. $BTC
items.tweetB: Bear-market PTSD is a positioning input. If the survivors are still underweight because they remember the drawdown, the marginal buyer hasn't shown up yet. That's fuel, not a headwind.

items.title: AI won't fire you; it will 'kill the raise': output up, headcount flat, wages frozen
items.idea: BowTiedBull: the likely scenario is a slow bleed, not a jobs cliff. Example: a 5-person banking team automates 75% of the busy work, but AI doesn't create clients, so the MD and VP gain and associates/analysts get no raise. Entry level is commoditised first. Making 10 models instead of 5 doesn't add profit.
items.angle: Productivity without revenue means labor share falls even if employment holds. K-shape widens inside firms, not just between them.
items.tweetA: The AI jobs story isn't layoffs, it's a raise that never comes. 75% of analyst busy work automated, zero new clients. The value of that labor falls to zero without anyone getting fired. Productivity shows up in margins, not wages.
items.tweetB: If AI makes a banking analyst 4x faster and the MD has the same 100 clients, the firm needs a quarter of the analysts. The Street's cheapest cost line gets cut and nobody calls it layoffs. Attrition does it.

items.title: The arbitrage: use AI for the blue-collar tradesman who has no time for marketing
items.idea: BowTiedBull argues white-collar AI use is saturated (everyone has the same tools) while the trades are untouched. Suggested play: find a young, good painter with few clients and build his online profile, reviews and quoting for a slice of each new client. 'Marketing is the new software engineering.' The shift: value moves to getting customers, as building becomes commodity.
items.angle: Distribution beats production when production is free. Also hints that AI-adoption in trades is the underpenetrated vertical.
items.tweetA: Every white-collar worker has Claude. Almost no plumber does. The AI opportunity isn't selling automation to people who already have it, it's selling customers to people who have no time to find them.
items.tweetB: When software is free to write, the scarce asset is attention. That's why a painter with 12 clients and a good Google profile is a better AI business than another dashboard. Distribution is the new moat.
